I'm 58 years old this year, and I've been farming these flat lands in Quzhou for over thirty years. My family has about 8 mu of good farmland. Both my children work in Shijiazhuang now, so it's mostly me and my husband handling the farm work, though we hire machines for ploughing and harvest. 

This year I'm sticking with what I know best — winter wheat and summer maize on all 8 mu. I thought about planting cotton like my neighbor Lao Zhang, but honestly, my back can't take all the bending and hand-picking anymore, and cotton prices have been unpredictable. Wheat and maize are safe and can be mostly mechanized. The wheat went in last October after rotary tillage, and now in April it's greening up nicely. The extension agent told us about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I always put a bit more to be safe — I remember the year 2012 when I tried to save on fertilizer and the yield dropped by nearly a third. I'll topdress at jointing and irrigate four times total, including the winter irrigation I already did. Water costs money now that the electricity for the tube well is metered, but dry soil means empty grain heads. For pests, I'll spray about four times — herbicide once in spring, then insecticide and fungicide when I see aphids or rust spots.

After wheat harvest in early June, there's barely a week before we must plant maize. No time to plough — the machine sows directly into the wheat stubble. I'll buy hybrid maize seed, one package per mu. The compound fertilizer goes down at planting, and maize grows fast in summer heat so two irrigations and three pesticide sprays should be enough. I expect about 420 kg per mu for wheat and 480 kg per mu for maize if the weather cooperates. It's not the highest yield in the village, but it's steady, and at my age, steady is what keeps food on the table.

I apply slightly more nitrogen than the extension recommendation because I am loss-averse — a yield drop hurts more than the cost of extra fertilizer. I use rotary tillage for wheat in autumn but no-tillage for summer maize because the turnaround between wheat harvest and maize sowing is less than one week. I irrigate wheat four times including winter irrigation because groundwater pumping is costly but essential on the North China Plain, while maize only needs two summer irrigations. My yield expectations are moderate but steady, reflecting my conservative approach at this stage of life."
